text.p: Maybe you'll make a bucket of money betting on this year's election returns, but then where would you invest it?

Conventional wisdom holds that financial markets tend to do poorly in years following Presidential elections, and as most market observers are happy to tell you, this bull market is getting kind of old.

But the same observers have studied the statistics that link stocks, bonds and election results, and they are not particularly worried. Here's a quick guide to what you can expect from the markets once Tuesday's results come in.

If President Clinton wins re-election and both houses of Congress stay Republican, expect stock traders to roll over and catch another 40 winks before they start trading on Wednesday morning. This is exactly what Wall Street is expecting as well as what it wants, said New York money manager Gerard Breitner, president of Excomp Asset Management.

A Republican Congress unlikely to spend money and a Democratic president unlikely to hand out big tax cuts is the best fiscal combination, so when Wall Street does start trading post-election, expect the short-term drift to be upward.

Where should you concentrate your buying? Look again at small company stocks, which went up 21 percent in the first year of Clinton's presidency, compared with the 10 percent gains posted by blue chips.

Democrats in general, and Bill Clinton in particular, tend to favour policies that help smaller, fast growing companies. Mike Braude, president of the Kansas City Board of Trade, pointed to this effect, and noted that small stocks often have a January bounce, known as the "January effect," regardless of who is in the White House.
What about sectors? The expected Clinton win will be good for high technology, managed care and multinational companies, said Albert Golly, a New York investment advisor.
If Clinton's win is so strong he sweeps the House and/or the Senate with him, don't look for such a sanguine Wall Street.

"I would sell all my bonds immediately," said Breitner. Investment professionals see an all-Democrat Washington as too easy on inflation; government spending would rise, pushing interest rates up higher too, they said.
Breitner said this scenario could result in a Wednesday morning washout that would drop the Dow as much as 500 points before stocks stopped falling.

To protect against such a free-fall, Breitner suggested investments in mutual funds that buy international stocks or real estate investment trusts, or those that take contrary approaches to the market.

The worst place to be if the market turns against you is in an index fund. These funds, which attempt to replicate broad stock market indexes, such as the Standard and Poor's 500 stocks, have no any downside protection.
What if Bob Dole does the unexpected? Don't expect Wall Streeters to be happy, even though many of them may vote for him.

A Republican win could cause a lot of frenzied activity in the market Wednesday, just because it is so unexpected. Stocks could fall on fears that Dole and a Republican Congress would push through tax cuts that could worsen deficits, raise interest rates and hurt the economy, traders said.
But certain stocks might do better: those of big blue-chip companies, energy producers and tobacco companies, which are spending megabucks to fight a Clinton crackdown on cigarettes.
Finally, feel free to ignore all of these morning after manipulations, especially if you're invested for the long term and you don't let day to day moves shake up your portfolio.
